```toml
go.pkg-path = "go"

[build]
command = """
  CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o "$out/bin/myapp" ./...
```

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| `go.runtime = false` | Nix/Flox treats `go` as a build-input only; it is present during `flox build` but pruned from the runtime closure entirely. |

| `$out/bin/myapp` | Flox sets `$out` to the Nix store output path; anything placed there becomes the package contents. |

## The root cause

Nix's closure scanner finds `/nix/store/<hash>-go-<version>/` strings embedded in your binary — from DWARF debug info, GOROOT paths in `runtime/debug.BuildInfo`, and CGO wrapper references. Any match pulls the full toolchain in.

Three build flags eliminate all of these vectors.

---

## Complete solution

```toml
version = 1

[install]
go.pkg-path = "go"

[build.myapp]
  command = '''
    CGO_ENABLED=0 go build \
      -trimpath \
      -ldflags="-s -w" \
      -o "$out/bin/myapp" \
      .
  '''
```

---

## Commands

```bash
# Build the artifact
flox build

# Inspect the runtime closure — should contain only your binary and glibc
nix path-info -r ./result
```

---

## What each flag does

| Flag | What it removes from the binary |
|---|---|
| `CGO_ENABLED=0` | C library links and CGO wrapper paths; produces a fully static binary |
| `-trimpath` | All absolute source paths (GOROOT, module cache) from DWARF and `debug.BuildInfo` — the single most important flag |
| `-ldflags="-s -w"` | Symbol table (`-s`) and DWARF debug sections (`-w`); eliminates the remaining path-embedding vectors |

## Root cause

In Nix-based (Flox) environments, `gcc` is a **wrapped compiler** — the wrapper script injects correct `-I` and `-L` flags at compile time. Two things typically break C++ even after `flox install gcc`:

1. **Missing `binutils`** — the wrapper-gcc calls `ld` from `binutils`; without it the linker can't find symbols.
2. **`libstdc++.so` not on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`** — headers are found at compile time (the wrapper handles that), but the shared runtime library must be discoverable when the binary actually runs.

---

```toml
[install]
gcc.pkg-path     = "gcc"
binutils.pkg-path = "binutils"
gnumake.pkg-path  = "gnumake"    # remove if using cmake or another build system

[vars]
CC  = "gcc"
CXX = "g++"

[hook]
on-activate = """
  # The nixpkgs gcc wrapper sets compile-time include/lib paths automatically.
  # We only need to expose libstdc++.so for *runtime* dynamic linking.
  _libstdcxx="$(g++ --print-file-name=libstdc++.so.6 2>/dev/null)"

    export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$(dirname "$_libstdcxx")${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"
  fi
  unset _libstdcxx
"""
```

## Root Cause

In Flox (which is Nix-backed), the `gcc` package ships as a **wrapped compiler**. The wrapper scripts inject the correct `-isystem` flags for C++ headers (pointing into `/nix/store/.../include/c++/...`) and `-L` flags for `libstdc++` — but **only when the environment is activated**. Outside of `flox activate`, those wrapper scripts aren't on `PATH`, so even if `gcc` is installed, the system `gcc` (or nothing) is found instead, and standard library headers don't resolve.

---

## The Fix

### `manifest.toml`

```toml
version = 1

[install]
gcc.pkg-path       = "gcc"       # includes g++, libstdc++, and the cc-wrapper
binutils.pkg-path  = "binutils"  # ld, ar, etc.
gnumake.pkg-path   = "gnumake"   # make

[vars]
CC  = "gcc"
CXX = "g++"
```

`binutils` is needed because the Nix-wrapped linker (`ld`) also needs to find `libstdc++`; without it you can get symbol-resolution errors at link time even when compilation succeeds.

The right section is **`[profile]`**. Profile entries are shell scripts that are *sourced* into the user's shell on activation, so shell variable expansion works normally.

---

## The manifest

```toml
version = 1

[install]
# your packages here

common = """
  export PATH="$FLOX_ENV_PROJECT/node_modules/.bin:$PATH"
"""

[options]
systems = ["aarch64-darwin", "x86_64-darwin", "aarch64-linux", "x86_64-linux"]
```

`$FLOX_ENV_PROJECT` is a variable Flox sets automatically — it points to the directory containing `.flox/`, i.e. your project root. This is more robust than a bare `./node_modules/.bin`, which would only work if your CWD happens to be the project root when a shell command runs.

## Turning Your Flox Environment Into a Local Docker Image

No Dockerfile, no registry push needed.

### Manifest (`manifest.toml` — optional `[containerize.config]` block)

```toml
[containerize.config]
cmd = ["your-entrypoint", "arg"]   # omit to get an interactive shell
working-dir = "/app"
exposed-ports = ["8080/tcp"]
user = "1000:1000"
```

The `[containerize.config]` block is entirely optional. If you omit it, `flox containerize` still works — the container just drops you into an activated shell when you `docker run -it` it.

### The single command

```bash
flox containerize --runtime docker
```

That's it. Flox builds the image and loads it directly into your local Docker daemon — no `.tar` file, no `docker load`, no registry.

**What it does:** reads your `.flox/env/manifest.toml`, builds a hermetic image with all your packages and activation hooks baked in, and calls `docker load` under the hood. The resulting image runs `flox activate` as its entrypoint, so every package and env variable is available inside the container exactly as it is in your dev shell.
